tip: Language names stay lowercase in Portuguese: 'português' and 'inglês' take no capital, unlike in English.
'Conhecer' means to know in the sense of being familiar with a place or person. 'Saber' is for knowing facts or how to do something.
'Devagar' means slowly and is already an adverb, so it never takes the '-mente' ending.
'Nas' is 'em' plus 'as' (in or on the, feminine plural): 'nas redes sociais'.
'Pegar trânsito' is a very Brazilian expression meaning to get stuck in traffic. 'Pegar' is one of the most versatile verbs in Brazilian Portuguese.
Use 'estar', not 'ser', for where someone is right now: 'está no escritório' places him at the office at this moment.
'Ter preguiça de' means 'to feel lazy about' – yet another common 'ter' expression for states and feelings.
'Trazer' is to bring toward you, here: 'posso trazer um amigo'. Use 'levar' instead for taking something away from where you are.
'Fazer falta' means to be missed: 'ele faz falta' = the team misses him. Literally it means to make lack.
'Conhecer' is to meet someone for the first time or to know a person, not to know a fact.
Sunday 'churrasco' (barbecue) is a beloved Brazilian tradition – it's the main social gathering of the week for many families.
'A gente' (literally 'the people') = informal 'nós' (we). It takes the he/she verb form: 'a gente vai', not 'a gente vamos'. Brazilians say this all the time.
Portuguese has no apostrophe-s. Show possession with 'de' ('dos' = 'de' + 'os'): 'os textos dos alunos' = the students' texts.
'Irmãos' is masculine plural but can mean siblings of mixed gender, not only brothers.
'Ter que' + infinitive means 'to have to.' It's the most common way to express obligation in Brazilian Portuguese, more than 'dever.'
'Dizer' is irregular: 'eu digo', 'ele diz'. Here 'diz' means says.
'Quero um café' is perfectly polite in Portuguese; add 'por favor' and it carries none of the bluntness English 'I want' would.
'Estar' plus an '-ndo' verb marks an action in progress: 'está trabalhando' is 'she is working' right now.
'Desde' marks a starting point in time, meaning since: 'desde a infância' = since childhood.
'Como vão as coisas' uses 'vão' (they go) to ask how things are going.
'Ir embora' means to leave or go away, not just to go somewhere: 'fomos embora' = we left.
'Sem' followed by an infinitive means without doing something: 'sem me despedir' = without saying goodbye.
'Carregar' means both to charge a device and to carry: 'carrego o celular' = I charge my phone.
'Trazer' (to bring) is irregular: 'eu trago', 'ele traz'. Here 'traz' = brings.
'Trem' is the Brazilian word for train. In Portugal, they say 'comboio.'
'Estar com vontade de' means 'to feel like doing something.' It's a common way Brazilians express cravings and desires.
'Costumar' + infinitive means 'to usually do something.' It's a very natural way to express habits in Portuguese.
'Tocar' is to play an instrument. For sports and games use 'jogar' instead.
Use 'jogar' for sports and games: 'jogam vôlei'. Musical instruments take 'tocar' instead.
'Passar roupa' means to iron clothes, literally to pass clothes.
